label: Jazz Workshop
rationale: Charlie Parker's working quintet of 1948 — Miles Davis, Duke Jordan, Tommy Potter and Max Roach — captured live at the Onyx Club on West 52nd Street, New York, in July 1948 on a non-professional tape machine, and first issued in December 1957 as Jazz Workshop JWS 501 (S2, S3, S4, S5). The 15 grooves document the Parker–Davis bebop partnership in its natural club habitat — '52nd Street Theme', 'Shaw 'Nuff', 'Hot House', 'A Night in Tunisia', 'Chasin' the Bird', 'Dizzy Atmosphere' and 'How High the Moon' — though several tracks are incomplete because the taper concentrated on Parker's solos to conserve tape (S2, S3). Wikipedia describes the issuing Jazz Workshop label as Charles Mingus' (S2). AllMusic styles the album Bop, Jazz Instrument and Saxophone Jazz (S1), and Discogs styles it Bop (S4) — matching style_primary 'bebop'. Scott Yanow's AllMusic review finds that Parker 'plays quite brilliantly on this live set' while the recording quality 'sometimes borders on the unlistenable', making it 'for true Charlie Parker completists only' (1.5 stars); The Rolling Stone Album Guide gives 2.5 stars (S1, S2). The album's provenance is unusually layered and is recorded as content in the dossier: the tape is credited to trombonist Jimmy Knepper by the 1994 CD reissue liner notes (S2) but to Dean Benedetti's private tape by Discogs and the Losin sessionography (S5, S6), and the liner notes themselves allow that the recording might have been made at the nearby Three Deuces rather than the Onyx Club (S2) — while the sessionographies place it at the Onyx Club on July 6, 1948 (S3, S4, S6). Reissued on Fantasy 6011 (1964), America 30 AM 6061 (France, 1969), Debut/Fantasy VIJ-5014M/DEB-5014 (Japan, 1976) and Original Jazz Classics OJC-114/OJCCD-114-2 (S3, S4).

personnel.notes: Listed as 'Kenny Pancho Hagood, vocal' for the Jazz Workshop JWS 501 session by jazzdisco (S3). No vocal is credited on the 1957 LP itself and its 15 issued tracks are instrumentals (S1, S2, S5), so track coverage is unknown. Conflict preserved as content: Losin lists Earl Coleman (voc) rather than Hagood for the same Onyx Club engagement on the Dean Benedetti tape (S6), and places Kenny 'Pancho' Hagood (voc) with this same quintet at the Three Deuces on March 31, 1948 (S7).

personnel_record.notes: One session per the album's sessionographies: Onyx Club, NYC, July 6, 1948 (S3; S2 infobox 'Recorded July 6, 1948'). Losin documents the quintet booked at the Onyx Club for six nights, July 6-11 (Tuesday-Sunday), with the surviving amateur tape covering at least four of those nights plus an afternoon rehearsal (S6); jazzdisco and Wikipedia date the JWS 501 material specifically to July 6. VENUE CONFLICT PRESERVED: Wikipedia, quoting the 1994 CD reissue liner notes, reports that the liner notes suggest the recording 'might have been recorded at the nearby Three Deuces club' (S2); the sessionographic consensus is the Onyx Club (S2 infobox, S3 'Onyx Club, NYC, July 6, 1948', S4 'recorded in performance at the Onyx, New York City, July 1948', S6). Both site_raw claims are recorded as separate recording_sites entries for the same session, both with epistemic 'unk' per the contract's conflict rule; the complete site_new (Onyx Club, 57 West 52nd Street) is attached to the sessionographic-consensus claim only. AllMusic gives only city-level 'New York, NY' (S1); the 1957 LP labels say 'Recorded in New York City, 1948' (S5). The Onyx Club of 1942-1949 stood at 57 West 52nd Street — the iteration that featured Parker; earlier Onyx Club addresses (35, 62, 72 West 52nd Street) predate this recording (S11). Coordinates geocoded from the documented address via scripts/geocode-place.py (rung 2, OSM Nominatim). TAPE-ATTRIBUTION CONFLICT PRESERVED: the 1994 CD reissue liner notes credit trombonist Jimmy Knepper with making the non-professional recording, focused on Parker's solos to conserve tape (S2); Discogs credits 'Recorded By [Uncredited] — Dean Benedetti' and 'Edited By — Jimmy Knepper' (S5); Losin identifies the July 6-11 Onyx material as a Dean Benedetti private tape (S6), on which ten of the album's performances were also issued on Fantasy OJCCD-114, the CD reissue of this album. PRODUCTION: no producer or engineer is documented in any source searched (S1-S7); explicit nulls with epistemic_production 'unk'. Production-side credits that do exist: Edited By — Jimmy Knepper; Technician [Technical Help] — Bob Guy; Recorded By [Uncredited] — Dean Benedetti; Cover — Scott Hyde and Tom Hannan (S5); Kirk Felton — Audio Restoration, Remastering for the CD era (S1). VOCALIST CONFLICT: jazzdisco lists 'Kenny Pancho Hagood, vocal' for the session (S3); the LP itself credits no vocal and its 15 grooves are instrumentals (S1, S2, S5); Losin lists Earl Coleman (voc) for the same engagement's Benedetti tape (S6) and Kenny 'Pancho' Hagood (voc) with this same quintet at the Three Deuces on March 31, 1948 (S7) — Hagood is carried as personnel with scope 'unknown' and epistemic 'unk'. SEVERAL TRACKS ARE INCOMPLETE: the taper started and stopped to capture Parker's solos (S2); the repeated tunes ('Out of Nowhere', 'This Time the Dream's on Me', '52nd Street Theme') are separate performances from the engagement, printed by jazzdisco with I/II designations (S3), not alternate takes of studio material. Titles: the 1957 LP labels print 'Theme' on the opening and closing grooves (A1/B7 per S5); '52nd Street Theme' is used per S1/S2/S3. Wikipedia's listing prints 'Dizzy at Atmosphere', a typo for 'Dizzy Atmosphere' (S3, S4, S5). COMPOSER VARIANCES RECORDED: 'Shaw 'Nuff' is printed Brown-Fuller-Gillespie (S1, S2) but credited Gillespie-Parker by Losin (S6); 'A Night in Tunisia' is credited to Gillespie (S2) with AllMusic adding Frank Paparelli (S1); 'Dizzy Atmosphere' is credited to Gillespie (S2) but Gillespie-Parker by Losin (S6, S7). Durations are from the Wikipedia track listing of the original LP (S2); AllMusic's durations differ by a few seconds (e.g. 2:17, 1:31, 3:02, 3:37) — reissue-transfer variance, not alternate takes. Wikipedia total 40:01 vs AllMusic 39:30. RELEASE: first issued December 1957 on Jazz Workshop JWS-501/JW-501, US (S2 citing Billboard December 23, 1957; S4; S5 viewed: 'Released: Dec 1957'); AllMusic dates the release 1958 (S1). Wikipedia describes the label as Charles Mingus' Jazz Workshop label (S2). Reissues: Fantasy 6011 (1964), America 30 AM 6061 (France, 1969), Fantasy/Debut VIJ-5014M/DEB-5014 (Japan, 1976), Original Jazz Classics OJC-114/OJCCD-114-2 (S3, S4). APPLE ALBUM ID: iTunes collectionId 1444030731 = 'Bird On 52nd Street (Remastered) [1948]', 15 tracks, release date 1957 — matched on artist, title, track count and the 1948/1957 dates (S10); it is the single remastered album, not a compilation or box. The 1957 JWS-501 original cover is documented at Discogs (not staged: i.discogs.com 403s to plain fetches, and the stager takes one art row): https://i.discogs.com/lWv4ZDBUMreIVtGixka7G09PBSTD03WJ9bXJ_QoZ6Rs/rs:fit/g:sm/q:40/h:300/w:300/czM6Ly9kaXNjb2dz/LWRhdGFiYXNlLWlt/YWdlcy9SLTQxNjUw/NjctMTUzMzA3OTA5/Ny01NjM4LmpwZWc.jpeg

ballot.case_for: This is unusually strong session-gravity evidence: Parker's 1948 working quintet with Miles Davis, Duke Jordan, Tommy Potter, and Max Roach is documented live in the 52nd Street club world, with the personnel and July 6 session supported by AllMusic, Jazz Discography Project, Discogs, and Peter Losin (S1, S3-S6). Performances of "Shaw 'Nuff," "Hot House," and "A Night in Tunisia" preserve Parker's club intensity and illuminate a formative Parker-Davis-Roach lineage, while the Jazz Workshop release adds historical interest as a musician-linked act of bebop dissemination (S2, S5).
ballot.case_against: The album fails the discovery test for many listeners: the amateur tape is sonically degraded, several performances are truncated or incomplete, and AllMusic's Scott Yanow calls the recording sometimes nearly unlistenable and recommends it mainly to Parker completists, while Rolling Stone gives it only 2.5 stars (S1, S2). Its value is primarily documentary rather than a defining Parker statement, and the dossier provides no Penguin Guide, NPR, DownBeat, or comparable canonical-list placement for this specific release. Venue and tape-attribution conflicts further weaken its status as a definitive artifact, even though the sessionographic consensus favors the Onyx Club and the Benedetti material (S2-S6).
ballot.disagreement: The references agree that the album is in scope and historically important but split on the verdict: Reference 1 finds the competing cases genuinely balanced and assigns contested/consider, while Reference 2 treats the poor sound, fragmented performances, and lack of canon-list recognition as decisive and assigns exclude_suggested/consider.
ballot.recommendation: John should consider it only as an archival, session-gravity document rather than as a primary Parker introduction, with inclusion depending on how much documentary bebop evidence the canon wants to preserve.
